response.message: We're building a Google Cloud pipeline that ingests synthetic sensor events, buffers and validates them, scores anomalies, stores results and alerts an operator. I've drawn it with Pub/Sub, Dataflow, Vertex AI, BigQuery and Cloud Monitoring. Our first local test would replay a fixed synthetic event file through a scripted mock model to check that device ID, timestamp and units survive end to end and that bad events go to the dead-letter topic. That only tests the plumbing: it says nothing about detection quality, and nothing is deployed or approved for any region or account yet. Will the synthetic events include labelled anomalies, so we can measure detection rate and false alarms against a time-based holdout?

proposal.title: GCP sensor anomaly detection – first end-to-end sketch
proposal.body: Scope: synthetic sensor events → Pub/Sub (durable buffer) → Dataflow validation (schema check that keeps device_id, timestamp and unit; rejected events go to a dead-letter topic) → Vertex AI online endpoint (anomaly score) → BigQuery results → Cloud Monitoring alert to an existing operator. Assumptions: the region is not chosen yet; the model is a placeholder until we agree on labels and evaluation; local tests use a mocked model. Native Terraform for these GCP services is not generated yet, so engineering work is still needed. Nothing has been deployed or verified.

data.label: Synthetic sensor event generator
data.description: Existing synthetic event producer, outside the provisioning scope. It sends JSON events with device_id, event timestamp, metric, value and unit.

data.label: Ingestion topic
data.description: Pub/Sub topic and subscription that durably buffer events with retention, so they can be replayed. The publisher authenticates with a scoped service account. device_id is the ordering key.

data.label: Validation & feature window
data.description: Validates the schema, unit whitelist and timestamp sanity, and keeps device_id, event time and unit unchanged. It builds per-device windows for scoring and sends rejected events to the dead-letter topic with a reason.

data.label: Rejected events (dead-letter)
data.description: Dead-letter topic for invalid or unprocessable events, kept for inspection and replay.

data.label: Anomaly scoring model
data.description: Returns an anomaly score and flag for each device window. In local tests it is a scripted mock. The real model, its training labels and its thresholds are not decided yet.

data.label: Anomaly results
data.description: Results table with device_id, event timestamp, unit, value, score, flag and model version, partitioned by event date.

data.label: Operator alerting
data.description: Raises an alert from a log-based metric on flagged anomalies. It also alerts on dead-letter backlog and pipeline lag.

data.label: Operator
data.description: Existing on-call person who receives alerts through an email or chat notification channel that is still to be confirmed.

requirementDrafts.rationale: If identity or units are lost, alerts can point to the wrong device or misread values.
requirementDrafts.basis: User: "Preserve device identity, timestamps and units."
requirementDrafts.statement: Every accepted event and result must keep the original device_id, event timestamp and unit unchanged from ingestion to the results table.

requirementDrafts.rationale: Without this, bad data either corrupts scores or disappears unnoticed.
requirementDrafts.basis: User asked for validation, durable buffering and an operator alert.
requirementDrafts.statement: Invalid events go to a dead-letter topic with a rejection reason. They are never silently dropped, and a growing backlog alerts the operator.

requirementDrafts.rationale: Too many false alarms will lead operators to ignore alerts, and missed anomalies defeat the purpose.
requirementDrafts.basis: User: "distinguish mocked model behavior from actual model validation".
requirementDrafts.statement: Proposed: before go-live, check the anomaly model on a time-based holdout with labelled anomalies and set acceptable detection and false-alarm rates. Mocked model tests are not evidence of model quality.

Do not just recite a checklist or demand that a junior developer repair product internals. Offer a concrete supported correction when possible; otherwise ask one focused question and explain why its answer matters. Help improve this architecture from its current emulation results. Diagnose the first actionable finding. Propose a minimal supported architecture correction only when requirements already justify it; otherwise ask one precise question.
Preserve all required components, existing systems, IDs, established service choices, access boundaries and requirements. Never clear unfinished-work gates, remove workload scope, weaken tests or invent successful validation. A graph proposal cannot repair generator/runtime source or an emulator defect: identify that as product engineering work with a reproducer. Model output is not test evidence. A local emulation pass is not a cloud plan or deployment. After an applied correction, rerun emulation on the new artifact; do not reuse this result. response.message: Good news first: the emulation shows no failures. The design itself held together, and all 8 components and their links were accepted. It's still marked "blocked" because none of our Google Cloud pieces (Pub/Sub, Dataflow, Vertex AI, BigQuery, Cloud Monitoring) has a native generator or emulator implementation yet, and the two existing systems still need a reference plan. That's product engineering work for the GCP streaming path. We can't fix it by redrawing the diagram, and we shouldn't shrink the design to storage, so I've left the board unchanged. The reproducer for that work is revision 2, artifact 93206bc4…, with 8 "implementation needed" or "reference plan needed" gaps. To shape the first contract that engineering builds, will the synthetic events include labelled anomalies, so we can test the real model on a time-based holdout instead of only the mock?
